coredata.dc:description: Poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) possesses excellent film-forming ability and biodegradability. Therefore, it is considered to be a promising mulching film material that eliminates the need for recovery. In the applications that require PBAT degradation in the field after use, it is important to understand the biodegradation mechanism at moderate temperatures. We have previously isolated from the soil the mesophilic actinobacteria Rhodococcus fascians NKCM2511 that biodegraded PBAT under moderate temperature conditions (20–30 °C). In this study, to clarify the mechanism of PBAT degradation by the strain NKCM2511, a DNA fragment carrying the gene pbathRf responsible for the PBAT degradation activity was cloned. The gene encoded a 216-amino-acid-long protein designated as PBATH Rf . Homology modeling revealed that PBATH Rf belongs to the α/β hydrolase fold family, lacking the lid domain covering the active site. PBATH Rf degraded PBAT film at 30 °C at the rate of 0.10 ± 0.03 mg/cm2/d and was capable of degrading several other aliphatic polyester films. Liquid chromatography revealed that PBATH Rf preferentially cleaved the ester bond between 1,4-butanediol and adipic acid rather than that between 1,4-butanediol and terephthalic acid (T). This characteristic of PBATH Rf may explain the low degradation rate of the aliphatic-aromatic copolyester PBAT, compared to the rate of degradation of aliphatic polyesters without T. In addition, liquid chromatography showed that PBATH Rf released T, mono(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalic acid, and bis(2-hydroxybutyl) terephthalate from an amorphous poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) film. However, no significant change in the PET film surface after the treatment with PBATH Rf was found by scanning electron microscopy. This is the first report of an enzyme from the mesophilic actinobacteria Rhodococcus fascians that can hydrolyze various polyesters, including PBAT, and catalyze hydrolysis on the surface of an amorphous PET film. This study also provides insight into the biodegradation mechanism of PBAT in the actual field as it describes an enzyme from a naturally occurring organism that acts in the medium temperature range.

ce:section.ce:para: Poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) is an aliphatic-aromatic copolyester designed as a biodegradable polymer with high flexibility and good mechanical properties, similar to low-density polyethylene [1,2]. These beneficial properties warrant the use of PBAT as a potentially useful packaging material in food industries and as a mulch film in agricultural fields [3,4]. In microbiologically active environments, such as the soil and compost, biodegradable polyesters, including PBAT, are hydrolyzed not only chemically but also enzymatically, and become broken down on oligomeric and monomeric fragments [5,6]. Subsequently, microorganisms mineralize the released compounds, eventually producing biomass, water, and carbon dioxide under aerobic conditions and methane under anaerobic conditions [7,8].

The hydrolysis of biodegradable polyesters is catalyzed by the extracellular carboxylic ester hydrolases (EC 3.1.1), such as esterases, lipases, and cutinases. Among them, the thermostable enzymes produced by thermophiles, such as hydrolases from the bacterium Thermobifida fusca [9], cutinases from T. alba, T. cellulositylica, and the fungus Humicola insolens [10–12], and Cut190* from Saccharomonospora viridis AHK190 [13] , have been reported to be able to hydrolyze PBAT. In moderately aerobic conditions that exist in soil environments, fungi are the predominant PBAT degraders, whereas the role of bacteria in this process is minor [14]. Accordingly, several fungal enzymes derived from mesophilic fungi, such as FsC from Fusarium solani [15,16], PCLE from Paraphoma sp. B47–9 [17], and CfCLE from Cryptococcus flavus GB-1 [18], have been reported to degrade PBAT under such conditions. At the same time, only two PBAT-degrading enzymes produced by mesophilic bacteria, PBATH Bp from Bacillus pumilus NKCM3201 [19] and PpEst from Pseudomonas pseudoalcaligenes [20], have been reported to the best of our knowledge.

Biodegradation of PBAT occurs rapidly at the relatively high temperatures in the compost, whereas at moderate temperature conditions, the degradation is slower [21]. However, it is necessary to study PBAT degradation by enzymes derived from various microorganisms under moderate environmental conditions, because using PBAT as a mulch film necessitates its disposal in the environment [22].

In our previous study, we have studied in detail PBAT biodegradation mediated by the aerobic mesophilic strain Rhodococcus fascians NKCM2511, which belongs to the phylum Actinobacteria, isolated from a soil sample. The strain NKCM2511 degraded several polyesters, including PBAT, at mild temperatures (20–30 °C); furthermore, it was shown to constitutively express an extracellular PBAT-degrading enzyme [23]. To clarify the mechanism of PBAT degradation by the strain NKCM2511, in this study, we analyzed its genomic DNA sequence, isolated a gene responsible for PBAT degradation under moderate conditions, and biochemically characterized and modeled its protein product. In addition, the catalytic activity of the enzyme that enabled hydrolysis of a conventional aromatic polyester such as poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) was also investigated, as there have been reports that enzymes that hydrolyzed PBAT also showed hydrolytic activity toward PET [24,25].

To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first report of a PBAT-degrading enzyme cloned from an aerobic mesophilic actinobacterium. Furthermore, such studies of PBAT-degrading enzymes produced by a mesophilic bacterial PBAT degrader from the soil environment, provide useful insight for understanding the mechanisms of PBAT biodegradation in the field.

Poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT, ecoflex® Mn = 4.0 × 104, Mw/Mn = 2.1, Fig. 1 ), poly(butylene succinate-co-adipate) (PBSA, Mn = 3.4 × 104, Mw/Mn = 5.1), poly(butylene succinate) (PBSu, Mn = 3.7 × 104, Mw/Mn = 4.5), poly(epsilon-caprolactone) (PCL, Mn =1.5 × 104, Mw/Mn = 1.4), poly(ethylene succinate)(PESu, Mn = 1.5 × 104, Mw/Mn = 2.8), poly(lactic acid) (PLA, LACEA H-100, Mn = 4.7 × 104, Mw/Mn = 1.6), and poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyhexanoate) (PHBH, Mn = 7.9 × 104, Mw/Mn = 2.9) were kindly provided from BASF Japan Ltd, Showa Highpolymer Co., Ltd, Daicel Corporation, NIPPON Shokubai Co., LDT., Mitsui Chemicals, Inc., and KANEKA CORPORATION. Poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) film (thickness 0.2 cm, NOVACLEAR® A3020) having low crystallinity was purchased from Mitsubishi chemical corporation. According to wide angle X-ray diffraction data measured with RIGAKU RINT2200VF (Figure S1), the PET film was determined to be amorphous because there is only a broad peak due to amorphous scattering and the diffraction peaks at the angles such as 2θ = 183, 2θ = 23°,and 2θ = 27° corresponding to (010), (110) and (100) reflections in crystalline PET, were not be found [26,27]. Molecular mass of each polymer was analyzed by gel permeation chromatography (GPC) [22]. PET oligomeric model substrates: mono(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (ET) and bis(4-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (ETE) purchased from Sigma-Aldrich japan, were used without further purification. PBAT oligomeric model substrates, bis(4-hydroxybutyl) terephthalate (BTB) and bis(4-hydroxybutyl) adipate (BAB), were synthesized according to the reference [19]. 1H NMR spectra were recorded at 400 MHz on a JNM-ECX400 NMR spectrometer (JEOL Ltd., Tokyo, Japan) in deuterated chloroform with tetramethyl silane as the internal standard (BTB; 1H NMR (400 MHz, CDCl3) δ 8.12 (s, 4H), 4.40 (t, J = 6.5 Hz, 4H), 3.75 (t, J = 6.4 Hz, 4H), 1.93–1.86 (m, 4H), 1.78–1.71 (m, 4H) ppm, BAB; 1H NMR (400 MHz, CDCl3) δ 4.12 (t, J = 6.4 Hz, 4H), 3.68 (t, J = 6.2 Hz, 4H), 2.34–2.31 (m, 4H), 1.77–1.60 (m, 12H)).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Bacterial strains, plasmids, and culture conditions
ce:section.ce:para: Bacterial strains and plasmids used in this study are list in Table 1 . LB medium(pH 7.5; components (g/L): HIPOLYPEPTON, 10; Yeast Extract, 5; NaCl, 5), rich medium(pH 7.0; components (g/L): Tryptone, 10; Yeast Extract, 5; NaCl, 5; glucose, 10) and M9 medium(pH 7.0; components (g/L): KH2PO4, 3; Na2HPO4∙12H2O, 6; NH4Cl, 1.0; 1 M MgSO4, 1; 1% vitamin B1, 1; 1 M CaCl2, 0.1; 2 M glucose, 5.6), were used for culture the microbes. Polymer containing medium was prepared as follow: polyesters dissolved in dichloromethane were emulsified with TOMY ultrasonic disruptor UD-200 in M9 medium containing 0.1% (w/v) Plysurf. Dichloromethane was removed by heating at 40 °C with a heating stirrer. In case of solid media, agar (15 g/L) was added.

The gDNA of strain NKCM2511 was extracted according to previously described [28]. The gDNA was sequenced using DNBSEQ-G400 (MGI Tech.) with 2 × 150 paired-end reads at the Bioengineering Lab. Co., Ltd., Kanagawa, Japan. Genome analyses were performed using the DOE Systems Biology Knowledgebase (KBase, http://kbase.us) [29]. The raw read data was uploaded with Import Paired-End Reads from Web (v1.0.12) in FASTQ format. Trimmomatic (v.0.36) was used to remove low-quality sequences and adapter sequences from the raw data to generate trimmed raw data [30]. SPAdes pipeline(v3.13.0) was used to assemble the trimmed data to generate the contigs [31]. RASTtk pipeline(v1.073) was used to annotate the assembly [32]. Using the Fast ANI pipeline(v.0.1.2) [33], we examined the homology between the genome assembly of strain NKCM2511(Genbank assembly accession: GCA_014905595.2), the genome assembly of R. fascians NBRC 12155(Genbank assembly accession: GCA_000761055.1, RefSeq assembly accession: GCF_001894785), and the complete genome of R. fascians D188(Genbank accession: CP015235.1, RefSeq assembly accession: GCF_001620305.1).

In order to identify PBAT hydrolase genes from annotated gDNA sequence of strain NKCM2511 using Blastp search in KBase, amino acid sequences of the previously reported PBAT hydrolases were used as query sequences. The open reading frame (ORF) of a hypothetical protein (locus tag: RN2511_028120) gene, designated as pbathRf, was amplified using the PCR method with two primers designed based on the genome sequence of the strain NKCM2511. Sequence alignment of the hypothetical protein, designated as PBATH Rf , with related enzymes was performed using ClustalW (https://clustalw.ddbj.nig.ac.jp). Molecular Evolutionary Genetic Analysis ver. 7 (MEGA7) was used to construct a dendrogram using the neighbor-joining algorithm [34,35]. The PCR reaction was performed using the gDNA of the strain NCKM2511 as a template, Gotaq® long Master Mixes (Promega KK) was use as DNA polymerase, along with a pair of primer (hp-F and gk-R). DNA fragments containing the ORF with its upstream and downstream alignments were ligated into vector pMD20 (the resulting plasmid was denoted as pMD-pbathRf , Table 1, Figure S2). PBAT hydrolytic activity by recombinant Escherichia coli DH5a-carrying pMD-pbathRf was confirmed by clear zone formation on M9 based PBAT-containing medium at 37 °C for 5 d.

The gene pbathRf encoding PBAT hydrolase PBATH Rf from strain NKCM2511 was codon optimized for heterologous expression in E.coli through overlap PCR method using mutagenic primers (Table 2 ). PCR mixture was as follows: pMD-pbathRf (100 pg), 5 × Q5 reaction buffer (4 µL), 2.5 mM dNTPs (2 µL), 5 × Q5 High GC enhancer (4 µL), Q5® High Fidelity DNA Polymerase (0.25 µL, 0.01 U), primer pairs (cut3F and G123C-R, and C141G-F and cut3R), and ddH2O (up to 20 µL). Thermal cycles were as follows: 1 cycle of 98 °C 2 min, 25 cycle of 98 °C for 30 s, 55 °C for 30 s, and 68 °C for 20 s, and 1 cycle of 68 °C for 5 min.

Then, Overlap PCR [36] was performed in order to ligate two of the DNA fragments (Figure S3). PCR mixture was as follows: each DNA fragment (1 µL), 5 × Q5 reaction buffer (4 µL), 2.5 mM dNTPs (2 µL), 5 × Q5 High GC enhancer (4 µL), Q5® High Fidelity DNA Polymerase (0.25 µL, 0.01 U), and ddH2O (up to 18 µL). Thermal cycles, were as follows: 1 cycle of 98 °C for 2 min, 10 cycle of 98 °C for 30 s, and 68 °C for 50 s. After Primers, cut3F, and cut3R (each, 1 µL), were added to the PCR mixture. PCR was performed to amplify the ligate that was generated, with the following thermal cycles: 20 cycles of 98 °C for 30 s, 55 °C for 30 s, and 68 °C for 20 s, and 1 cycle of 68 °C for 5 min. The amplified DNAs were ligated into pMD20 (resulting plasmid was donated as pMD-pbathRfxx). The change of codons was confirmed through DNA sequencing (Eurofins genomics K.K.). The codon optimized gene of pbathRf (pbathRfxx) excluding its deduced signal peptide was amplified by PCR with a pair of primer as forward primer (cut3F-ecoRI) containing restriction site of EcoRI, and reward primer (cut3R-hishind) containing six histidine residues (His6-tag) encoding the nucleotide sequence before the stop codon TGA with restriction site of HindIII (Figure S4). The PCR product was cloned into the EcoRI and HindIII restriction sites in multi-cloning site of pMAL-p2 vector, resulting in plasmid DNA (pMAL-pbathRf ). pMAL-pbathRf was introduced into E.coli Rosetta-gami™ B, resulting transformant E.coli pMAL-pbathRf . The transformant E.coli pMAL-pbathRf will express MBP-PBATH Rf , a fusion protein of PBATH Rf which fused maltose binding protein (MBP) at N-terminal, and His6-tag at C-terminal.

The transformant E. coli pMAL-pbathRf was aerobically incubated in 600 mL of rich medium supplemented with 50 µg/mL ampicillin at 37 °C till reaching cell density of OD600 = 0.4–0.6. Then, isopropyl-β-d-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) was added into the culture at a final concentration of 1 mM to induce the expression of the recombinant protein, and cultivation was continued at 37 °C for 3 h. Extraction of the recombinant protein MBP-PBATH Rf from the periplasmic space of E.coli was conducted according to manufactures’ instruction (New England BioLabs®). The transformant cells were harvested from the culture medium and resuspended in 200 mL of 30 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0 with 20% (w/v) sucrose and 0.4 mL of 0.5 M EDTA, pH 8.0, followed by shaking at room temperature for 10 min. The mixture was centrifuged at 8000 rpm for 20 min at 4 °C, and the pellet was resuspended in 200 mL of ice-cooling 5 mM MgSO4 followed with shaking at ice bath for 10 min. To harvest the supernatant (Osmotic shock extracted fraction), the sample was centrifuged again in the same conditions. Then, 1 M sodium phosphate buffer (pH 7.4) was added into the supernatant to final concentration at 20 mM sodium phosphate buffer. The supernatant was applied to 1 mL HisTrap-FF column (GE Healthcare) and washed with 10 vol of 20 mM sodium phosphate buffer containing 30 mM imidazole, and 500 mM NaCl (pH 7.4). The bound protein was eluted using 20 mM sodium phosphate buffer containing 500 mM NaCl, and 300 mM imidazole (pH 7.4). Then, five microliters of each fraction were dropped into emulsified PESu containing plate, and then the plate was incubated at 30 °C for 12–14 h to a formed clear zone. The fractions that exhibited the hydrolytic activity which was determined by the clear zone formation method were harvested. Then, 10 µg of protease Factor Xa was added into the harvest fraction, and incubated at 4 °C for 5 ds (MBP-PBATH Rf ). The protein solution was dialyzed in 200 mL of 10 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 7.0) at 4 °C for 2 h in two times. Thereafter, the protein solution was applied to HiTrap Q column to remove MBP, and the protease Factor Xa. The bound protein was eluted with 10 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 7.0) containing 100 mM NaCl using a linear gradient from 0 to 100 mM NaCl. The fractions that exhibited hydrolytic activity for PESu were pooled and concentrated using AQUA KEEP 60 (Sumitomo Seika Chemicals, Co., Ltd.), and then dialyzed against 1 L of 50 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 7.0) overnight at 4 °C. To confirm the purity of the protein, sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) with 13.5% (w/v) of acrylamide was conducted, followed by protein staining using a CBB staining kit (Rapid CBB KANTO, Kanto Chemical, Co., Inc.). Protein concentration was determined using the Bradford protein assay [37].

The deduced 3 catalytic residues; S114, D181, and H194 were substituted with Aln, Asn, and Asn, respectively. Three mutated genes, designated as pbathRf S114A, pbathRf D181N, and pbathRf H194N, were prepared using the overlap PCR method using mutagenic primers (Table 2) with pMD-pbathRfxx as a template (cf. experiment Section 2.3). The amplified genes were inserted into EcoRI and HindIII restriction sites in multi-cloning site of pMAL-p2 vector, resulting in plasmid DNAs; pMAL-pbathRf S114A, pMAL-pbathRf D181N, and pMAL-pbathRf H194N, respectively. The mutated genes were confirmed using DNA sequencing. The plasmid DNAs were introduced into E.coli Rosetta gami™ B resulting in three recombinants: E.coli pMAL-pbathRf S114A, E.coli pMAL-pbathRf D181N and E.coli pMAL-pbathRf H194N which produced PBATH Rf variants that fused with MBP, designate as MBP-PBATH Rf S114A, MBP-PBATH Rf D181N, and MBP-PBATH Rf H194N, respectively. To evaluated polyesters hydrolytic activity, the recombinants E. coli were cultured on polyesters containing agar plates at 37 °C for 5 ds. The three variant proteins were purified with the same procedure of MBP-PBATH Rf purification (cf. experiment Section 2.4). The hydrolysis activities of the three proteins were evaluated by clear zone formation on polyesters containing agar plates.

Six of p-nitrophenyl esters with different alkyl chains: p-nitrophenyl acetate (PNPA), p-nitrophenyl butyrate (PNPB), p-nitrophenyl caprylate (PNPC), p-nitrophenyl laurate (PNPL), p-nitrophenyl myristate (PNPM), and p-nitrophenyl palmitate (PNPP) were used in order to investigate esterase activity [19]. Time course of the absorbance at 405 nm for 5 min were monitored with reaction mixtures of 1 mL: 0.2 µg PBATH Rf of, 100 µL each substrate (1%(w/v) of the substrate solution which were adjusted with 1,4-dioxane and nonaethylene glycol monododecyl ether), and 900 µL of 50 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 7.0). Enzymatic unit (U) was defined as the activity of the enzyme that hydrolyze 1 µmol of p-nitrophenyl ester for 1 min at 30 °C in the buffer. Mole number of p-nitrophenol (PNP) was calculated using Lambert-Beer law (c = A/εl, A: absorbance at 405 nm c: concentration of the release PNP, ε: extinction coefficient, 1.85 × 104 lmol−1 cm−1, l: cell length (1 cm))[19].

To investigate thermal stability of the enzyme, 0.2 µg of PBATH Rf was incubated at 4, 10, 20, 25, 30, 37, 50, and 60 °C for 30 min. To investigate pH stability, 0.2 µg of PBATH Rf was incubated in several buffers at 30 °C for 3 h, following with the residue activity of the enzyme was determined using PNPB.

The effect of metal ions and chemical reagents on the enzymatic activity were evaluated by residual activities determination using PNPB. 0.2 µg of PBATH Rf was determining incubated with 1 equivalent numbers of the metal ions (KCl, MgCl2, CaCl2, MnCl2, and FeCl3) for 5 min at 30 °C. In addition, 0.2 mg of PBATH Rf was incubated with each chemical reagent: sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), diisopropyl fluorophosphate (DFP), dithiothreitol (DTT), phenylmethylsulphonyl fluoride (PMSF), and ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) at several concentrations for 30 min at 30 °C, following with the residue activity of the enzyme was determined using PNPB.

Polyesters (PBAT, PBSu, PBSA, PCL, PESu, PHBH, PLA and PET) films (1 × 1 cm with thickness 0.1 cm, except for PET film with thickness 0.2 cm) were put into 1 mL of 50 mM sodium phosphate (pH 7.0) containing 3.1 µg of PBATH Rf in 10 mL glass vials, respectively. As negative control, the films were added into the sodium phosphate (pH 7.0) without the enzyme. They were incubated at 30 °C with gentle shaking 50 strokes/min. The aliphatic polyesters films were incubated for 24 h. For PBAT and PET films, the films were incubated for 5 ds, and the enzyme solution was changed for every 24 h. The films were collected and wash with methanol and distilled water. After they were dried in vacuo, their weights loss was determined. Molecular masses of PBAT film were analyzed using gel permeation chromatography (GPC) (cf. experiment Section 2.1).

In order to confirm the degradation of PET, the supernatant of PET enzymatic degradation was applied to reverse-phase high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) with LC-2000 Plus series (PU- 2080 Plus; LG-2080; AS-2051 Plus; CO-2060 Plus; UV-2075 Plus, JASCO Corporation). Inert-Sustain® C18 column (3.0 µm, 2.1 × 150 mm) (GL Sciences Inc.) was used as the stationary phase. Then, 0.1% phosphoric acid solution (solution A) and acetonitrile (solution B) were used as the mobile phase with a flow rate of 0.2 mLmin−1 at 40 °C of column temperature. The chromatogram program was as followed: (1) 0 - 5 min (holding A 92% with B 8%), (2) 5 - 6 min (linear decrease A to 80%), (3) 6 - 13 min (linear decrease A to 70%, (4) 13 – 23 min (linear decrease A to 20%), and (5) 23 – 26 min (holding A 20% with B 80%).The eluted degrading products were detected using UV at a wavelength of 254 nm.

Surface morphology changes in PBAT and PET films before and after treatment with enzyme PBATH Rf were observed by SEM. The films were treated with 2.5% (v/v) glutaraldehyde for 1 h and wash with Milli-Q water. Then, they were soak in 50%, 60%, 70%, 80%, 90%, and 99.5% (v/v) ethanol for 20 min and t‑butyl alcohol for 60 min and finally dried in vacuo. The films, coated with Au-Pd using Magnetron Sputter MSP-1S, were observed with SEM (SSX-550, Shimadzu Co., Ltd.) at 15 kV of accelerating voltage.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Identification of PBAT enzymatic degradation products using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS)
ce:section.ce:para: The reaction supernatant was analyzed using LC-MS. The chromatographic separations of PBAT degrading products were performed using a Waters Acquity H-class UPLC system, equipped with a mobile-phase online degasser, quaternary pump, autosampler, column thermostat compartment, and diode array detector. Chromatography was achieved on an ACQUITY UPLC BEH C18 Column (1.7 µm, 2.1 × 100 mm) using linear gradients comprising of 0.1% formic acid in distilled water (mobile phase A) and 0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile (mobile phase B). The injection volume was fixed at 5 µL, the column temperature at 30 °C and the flow rate was set at 0.4 mLmin−1.The total run time was 14 min, and the gradients profile was as follows: (1) 0 – 8.0 min, linear decrease from 100% to 50% of A, (2) 8.0–9.0 min, linear decrease from 50% to 5% of A, and (3) 9.0–12.0 min, hold at 5% of A. MS detection was performed using a maXis HD ultra-high solution quadrupole time-of-life mass spectrometer with electrospray ionization mass (ESI) spectrometry in positive and negative ESI mode. The optimized source operating parameters were as follows: capillary voltage, 2.5 kV; cone voltage, 20 V; cone gas flow, 50 L/h; source temperature, 120 °C; desolvation temperature, 350 °C; desolvation gas flow, 350 L/h; Scan time, 0.1 s.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Degradation of PBAT oligomeric model substrates, BAB and BTB by PBATH Rf
ce:section.ce:para: The reaction mixture contained 1 mM of the model substrate, 1.0 µg PBATH Rf , and 10% (v/v) dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) in 1 mL of 50 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH7.0), and was shaken with 120 strokes.min−1 at 30 °C for 20, 40, 60, 120, and 180 min. As negative control, 1 mM of the model substrate were added into 50 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 7.0) containing 10% (v/v) DMSO without the enzyme. The reaction was stopped by the addition of 5 µL phosphoric acid. The reaction mixture was applied to HPLC to analyze the remaining of BAB and BTB. HPLC analysis conditions were similar to that of the PET degradation product as mentioned in the experiment Section 2.8, which UV wavelength was set at 210 nm for the detection of BAB and BTB.

ce:section.ce:section-title: 3D modeling of PBATH Rf and molecular docking
ce:section.ce:para: The 3D model of PBATH Rf was predicted using the SWISS-MODEL sever (https://swissmodel.expasy.org/) [38]. Cutinase Cut-Tr (PDB code: 4PSC) from the fungus Trichoderma reesei has 40.1% amino acid identity to PBATH Rf and highest similarity to PBATH Rf in the RCSB Protein Data Bank [39]. Therefore, Cut-Tr was used as a template to create a model structure of PBATH Rf . USCF Chimera program was utilized to visualize the predicted 3D structure of PBATHRf. Molecular docking was then performed using SwissDock sever (http://www.swissdock.ch) to analyze the likelihood of the PBATH Rf having the ability to bind to PBAT as a substrate [40]. BTB and BAB model substrates of PBAT, whose molecular data obtained from ZINC database (http://zinc.docking.org) and from ChemSpider (http://www.chemspider.com/), respectively, were used as ligands in the docking analysis. USCF Chimera program was used to visualize the binding model in more detail.

The whole genome shotgun project has been deposited in the DDBJ Sequence Read Archive (DRA) (BioProject ID PRJDB10459, Whole Genome Shogun (WGS) accession number: BNHJ00000000). pbathRf gene, codon optimized gene pbathRfxx for heterologous expression, and three of mutation genes were deposited in the DDBJ sequence database under accession numbers LC582818, LC582819, LC582820, LC582821, and LC582822.

The assembled genome size of the strain NKCM2511 had a total length of 5,285,001 bp, consisting of 26 contigs with the guanine plus cytosine content of 64.6%. There were 4976 annotated protein-coding genes. The average nucleotide identity (ANI estimated) analysis showed high similarity of the strain NKCM2511 with R. fascians NBRC 12155 (97.8%) and R. fascians D188 (97.7%).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Identification of the Rhodococcus fascians PBAT hydrolase PBATH Rf
ce:section.ce:para: The amino acid sequence analysis of the annotated genomic DNA sequences using blastp in the KBase platform indicated that the amino acid sequence of the hypothetical protein (locus tag: RN2511_028120), designated as PBATH Rf , showed a relatively high degree of homology with amino acid sequences of the reported PBAT-degrading enzymes such as HiC (PDBj code:4OYY) (32.7%) [12,41], PCLE (accession number: BAN51852) (29.0%) [17], CfCLE (accession number: BAT32793) (28.1%) [18] and FsC (PDBj code:1CEX) (27.6%) [16]. Moreover, our previous report suggested that a putative extracellular polyester hydrolase from the strain NKCM2511 had molecular weight of approximately 15 kDa according to the zymogram analysis of the culture supernatant, which is close to that of the hypothetical PBATH Rf protein (18,992 Da) [23]. Accordingly, we focused on this hypothetical protein encoded by the gene designated as pbathRf .

ce:section.ce:section-title: Cloning and heterologous expression of the pbathRf gene from Rhodococcus fascians
ce:section.ce:para: The targeted gene pbathRf was amplified by PCR with specific primers and cloned into the pMD20 plasmid, yielding the pMD-pbathRf plasmid. E. coli harboring pMD-pbathRf (E. coli pMD-pbathRf ) formed clear zones on the plates containing PBAT and aliphatic polyesters (PBSA, PBSu, PCL, and PESu) (Table S1). Fig. S5 shows the cloned DNA sequences. A total of 1465 bp of the cloned DNA sequence contained an open reading frame of pbathRf (651 bp) that encoded a protein with 216 amino acid residues. According to the amino acid sequence analysis by using signalP 5.0 server, the N-terminus of PBATH Rf contained a conserved 29-amino-acid-long signal peptide sequence. The molecular mass of the mature protein was estimated to be 18,992 Da based on the amino acid sequence. Upon a comparison of PBATH Rf and HiC amino acid sequences, residues S114, D181, and H194 were deduced as a putative catalytic triad. The lipase box G-X-S-X-G containing S114 was also present in the PBATH Rf amino acid sequence.

Fig. 2 shows a dendrogram based on the amino acid sequence of PBAT-degrading enzymes and other polyester hydrolases. As mentioned above, PBATH Rf exhibited relatively high similarity to PBAT hydrolases from fungi. Additionally, the amino acid sequence of PBATH Rf showed 30.3% similarity to that of a cutinase (AET25222) from R. fascians D188 [42]. On the other hand, PBATH Rf exhibited no significant similarity to several bacterial PBAT hydrolases such as BTA-hydrolase 1(TfH), Est1, and Est119 from Thermobifida species [10,11], PBATH Bp from Bacillus species [19], PpEst from Pseudomonas species [20], PfL1 from Pelosinus species [43], or Cbotu_EstA, Cbotu_EstB, and Chath_Est from Clostridium species [44,45].

ce:section.ce:section-title: Purification of the recombinant PBATH Rf
ce:section.ce:para: The transformant, E.coli pMAL-pbathRf , expressed the recombinant protein MBP-PBATH Rf . Crude proteins extracted from the periplasmic space of the strain were purified with a HisTrap column. The SDS-PAGE analysis revealed that proteins in the fractions with polyester hydrolytic activity had a single band with a molecular mass of approximately 60 kDa (Fig. 3 , lane 2), suggesting that they were MBP-PBATH Rf , MBP (42 kDa) with PBATH Rf (18.9 kDa). The purified fusion protein MBP-PBATH Rf was cleaved with protease Factor Xa to separate MBP from PBATH Rf . Digestion was confirmed by the SDS-PAGE analysis, in which two bands of proteins (approx. 40 and 18 kDa) were observed (Fig. 4 , lane 3). The eluted fraction was applied to a Hitrap Q column, resulting single band of approximately 18 kDa in the SDS-PAGE analysis corresponding to PBATH Rf fused with a His6 tag at the C-terminus (18.9 kDa). The recombinant enzyme was recovered from the fraction extracted by osmotic shock with a final recovery ratio of 30% and a 5.2-fold enrichment ratio (Table S2).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Characterization of the recombinant PBATH Rf
ce:section.ce:para: Then, the properties of the recombinant PBATH Rf fused with a His6-tag were studied. The enzyme preferentially hydrolyzed p-nitrophenyl esters with shorter acyl chain lengths. Among all p-nitrophenyl esters used in this study, PNPB underwent the highest degree of hydrolysis by PBATH Rf (Fig. S6). The activity of PBATH Rf toward PNPB was relatively high at a temperature range of 4–30 °C (Fig. S7). The activity of PBATH Rf dramatically decreased to 5% after incubation at 50 °C for 30 min and completely disappeared following incubation at 60 °C for 30 min. PBATH Rf showed relatively high stability at a range of pH values from 7.0 to 9.0, whereas under acidic conditions (pH 3.0–6.0), its activity was relatively low (Fig. S8).

The effects of several chemical reagents on the PBATH Rf enzymatic activity were then investigated. SDS and EDTA did not significantly affect the activity, whereas DFP, PMSF, and DTT remarkably inhibited it. The activity decreased to 14.6%, 77.1%, and 22.4% of the control value in the presence of 0.05 mM DFP, 1 mM PMSF, and 1 mM DTT, respectively (Table S3). The enzymatic activity was not affected by the presence of K+ and Mg2+ at molar quantities equal to that of the enzyme, but it was influenced by Ca2+, Mn2+, and Fe3+. The activity slightly increased the presence of Ca2+ to 104%, but it decreased when EDTA, a divalent metal ion-chelating agent was added (Table S4).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Identification of the catalytic sites in PBATH Rf
ce:section.ce:para: Codons encoding residues S114, D181, and H194 in PBATH Rf , deduced as the catalytic triad based on the similarity of the sequence to those of other PBAT-degrading enzymes, were respectively replaced by those encoding A114, N181, and N194 by PCR-based site direct mutagenesis. The three variants of PBATH Rf, which were fused with MBP yielding MBP-PBATH Rf S114A, MBP-PBATH Rf D181N, and MBP-PBATH Rf H194N, did not form clear zones on any of the polyester-containing plates, whereas MBP-PBATH Rf and PBATH Rf formed clear zones on the plates containing polyesters (PBAT, PBSu, PBSA, PCL, and PESu) (Table 3 ).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Enzymatic degradation of PBAT and other polyester films by PBATH Rf
ce:section.ce:para: The weight losses of polyester (PBAT, PESu, PBSA, PCL, and PBSu) films were remarkable after the treatment with PBATH Rf , with degradation rates of 0.10 ± 0.03, 2.51 ± 0.31, 2.42 ± 0.04, 1.92 ± 0.23, and 0.34 ± 0.05 mg/cm2/d, respectively (Fig. 4). On the other hand, we did not find significant weight losses in PLA or PHBH after the treatment with the enzyme. These results were in good agreement with those of the clear zone formation tests on polyester-containing plates (Table 3). As for the PBAT film degradation by PBATH Rf , there was no visible change after treatment with PBATH Rf after 1 d, whereas the film became opaque after incubation for 5 d (Fig. 5 (1)). Fig. 5(2) shows the SEM images of the PBAT film surfaces before and after the incubation with or without PBATH Rf for 1 and 5 d. Some cracks were found on the surface following the incubation for 1 d with the enzyme. Subsequently, the roughness of the surfaces increased after the incubation with the enzyme for 5 d. Additionally, the molecular mass of the PBAT film slightly decreased after the incubation at 30 °C for 5 d with the enzyme (Table S5).

PBATH Rf hardly reduced the weight of the PET, PLA, or PHBH films (0.01 ± 0.005, 0.02 ± 0.01, and 0.00 ± 0.01 mg/cm2/d). Furthermore, HPLC analysis revealed that the peaks that were assigned to terephthalic acid (T, 0.82 ± 0.13 µM), ET (4.22 ± 0.65 µM), and ETE (0.42 ± 0.04 µM) were detected in the supernatants after the amorphous PET film was incubated with PBATH Rf for 1 d (Fig. S9). However, the SEM analysis of the films revealed no significant alterations of their surfaces, despite the films were incubated with PBATH Rf for 5 d (data not shown).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Determination of PBAT degradation products by LC-MS
ce:section.ce:para: After the incubation of the PBAT film with PBATH Rf at 30 °C for 1 d, hydrolysates released into the supernatant were identified by LC-MS by using both negative and positive ion mode ESI. Fig. S10 shows PBAT degradation products determined by the LC-MS analysis. Detected m/z spectra were presumed to be 1,4-butanediol (B), adipic acid (A), T, and PBAT oligomers (AB, TB, BTB, ABA, TBA, TBT, BTBA (or BABT), and TBTB).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Degradation of PBAT oligomeric model substrates by PBATH Rf
ce:section.ce:para: The amount of BAB and BTB after incubation with PBATH Rf was determined by calculating the peak area of each substrate according to the HPLC profile. Although BTB amount slowly decreased with the incubation time, 95% of it was still present after the incubation for 180 min. Meanwhile, the amount of BAB decreased by more than 20% already within 20 min, and this substrate almost completely disappeared (by more than 95%) when the incubation lasted for 180 min (Fig. 6 ).

Fig. 7 shows the predicted 3D model structure of PBATH Rf and molecular docking. As the template structure, cutinase Cut-Tr was used in which a small lid domain covers the active site. Comparison of the amino acid sequences of PBATH Rf and Cut-Tr revealed that PBATH Rf lacked the homologous region of the lid domain of Cut-Tr at the N-terminus (Fig. S11). PBATH Rf likely belongs to the α/β hydrolase fold family, whose members have four alpha helices and five beta sheet strands. The deduced catalytic triad S114, D182, and H194 was found at the surface of the structure. Moreover, the positions of the residues C32-C103 and C177-C184 enable the formation of disulfide bonds.

The molecular docking experiment with SwissDock generated a binding mode with the smallest binding energy (ΔG) of −7.24 and −38.76 kcal/mol for BTB and BAB, respectively. The docking model constructed by the UCSF Chimera software showed that the substrates were able to fit into a groove with the active site S114 (marked in red), hydrophobic amino acids T43, F80, V183, F189, and L195 (marked in green), and polar amino acids E45 and N190 (Fig. 7b).

In our previous study, we have described the mesophilic terrestrial actinobacteria R. fascians NKCM2511 that degraded PBAT at mild conditions. In the present study, a genomic analysis of the strain NKCM2511 was performed, the gene responsible for PBAT degradation was cloned, and its product was biochemically characterized to elucidate the mechanism of the enzymatic degradation of PBAT.

ANI values in pairwise comparisons of the draft genomes of the strain NKCM2511, R. fascians NBRC12155, and R. fascians D188, were all higher than 97%. ANI value is widely used as an alternative to DNA-DNA hybridization to estimate the similarity on the species level. When ANI value is higher than 95%, it is likely that both organisms belong to the same species [33]. The results suggest that the strain NKCM2511 belongs to R. fascians, which agrees with 16S rDNA sequence data from our previous report [23].

The amino acid sequence of the hypothetical protein PBATH Rf deduced from the annotated genomic DNA of the strain NKCM2511 was more similar to those of the fungal PBAT-degrading enzymes, HiC [12,41], PCLE [17], CfCLE [18], and FsC [15,16] rather than of the bacterial enzymes (Fig. 2). The recombinant plasmid harboring PBATH Rf-encoding gene pbathRf triggered clear zone formation on PBAT-containing plates (Table S1), indicating that the pbathRf gene product PBATH Rf conferred PBAT hydrolytic ability upon the host strains. Therefore, pbathRf is responsible for the PBAT-degrading activity of the strain NKCM2511.

The mutational analysis showed that S114, D181, and H194 in PBATH Rf formed a catalytic triad. Additionally, its esterase activity was sensitive to serine hydrolase inhibitors such as PMSF and DFP [46,47], indicating that PBATH Rf is a serine hydrolase in which the S114 is a nucleophile for the carbonyl carbon in the ester bond with the substrate. Homology 3D structure modeling of PBATH Rf (Fig. 7) showed that it lacked the lid domain covering the active site. In general, the mobile lid domain promotes the enzymatic activity of lipases at the lipid-water interface [48]. In contrast, the absence of the lid domain in enzymes such as cutinase [50] and PETH_IDESA (PETase, PET hydrolase from I. sakaiensis) [49], whose substrates are water-insoluble, would be advantageous for the hydrolytic activity at solid-liquid interfaces [50,51]. The molecular docking model of PBATH Rf with a PBAT oligomeric substrate, such as BTB or BAB, revealed that the substrate-binding pocket around the active site S114 is large enough to accommodate the oligomeric substrates, which may explain why PBATH Rf can hydrolyze PBAT.

The enzyme showed higher substrate specificity for alkyl esters with relatively short chain length such as PNPA, PNPB, and PNPC (Fig. S6), and its hydrolytic activity to olive oil remained stable in alkaline conditions (Fig. S8). Such properties were similar to those of cutinase [50] and subfamily I.4 lipase with the smallest molecular mass in triacylglycerol lipase [52,53,19]. Taken together, the structural and functional similarities of this enzyme with cutinases suggests that PBATH Rf should be classified as a type of cutinase-like enzyme [50].

PBATH Rf degraded solid substrates, such as PBAT film, under mild conditions at 30 °C. Considering that PBATH Rf maintained the activity at temperatures below 30 °C, the enzyme likely expresses the PBAT-degrading activity under actual field conditions. In addition, the changes in the surface morphology of the PBAT film after the incubation with the enzyme (Fig. 5) and with the strain NKCM2511 [23] were similar. Taken together, we conclude that PBATH Rf is responsible for PBAT degradation by the strain NKCM2511 in actual conditions at the medium temperature range.

The fact that the enzyme activity is suppressed by the reducing agent DTT [54] suggests the presence of disulfide bonds in the molecule that maintain the highly ordered structure of the active form of the enzyme. This is consistent with the high-order structure predicted by the model structural analysis of PBATH Rf , in which disulfide bonds may form between the N-terminal residues C32 and C103 as well as between C177 and C184 close to the active site (Fig. 7). In the extracellular enzymes such as PETH_IDESA [49] and ThCut2 (cutinase from T. fusca KW3) [55], disulfide bonds regulate the thermal stability of the enzymes. In addition, a disulfide bond near the active site of PETH_IDESA endows it with higher flexibility at room temperature, which results in a higher degrading activity of PETH_IDESA compared to that of other PET-degrading enzymes without disulfide bonds near the active site [49,56]. The degradation rate of PBAT (0.10 ± 0.03 mg/cm2/d) by PBATH Rf , harboring disulfide bonds, is comparable to that achieved by the mesophilic PBAT hydrolase PCLE [17] that also has disulfide bonds in the molecule. PBATH Rf degraded PBAT films about 7.1 times faster than PBAT hydrolase PBATH Bp from the mesophilic B. pumilus NKCM3201, which does not have disulfide bonds in the enzyme structure [20]. On the other hand, the degradation rate of PBAT by PBATH Rf was much lower than that afforded by thermophilic PBAT-degrading enzymes, such as Cut190* from S. viridis AHK190 [13] (approx. 9-fold lower per the same enzyme amount) and TfH from T. fusca [9] (approx. 34-fold lower per the same enzyme amount). These observations may be related to the fact that PBAT shows good biodegradability under high temperature conditions, such as inside compost, but only very slow biodegradability under moderate temperature conditions, such as those in the field.

HPLC analysis showed that PBATH Rf exhibited weak catalytic activity hydrolyzing aromatic polyester amorphous PET films at 30 °C. The fungal cutinase FsC with PBAT hydrolyzing activity also showed hydrolytic activity toward an amorphous PET film at moderate temperatures [57,24]. However, the weight loss of PET following exposure to PBATH Rf was much lower (0.01 ± 0.005 mg/cm2/d) than that of PBAT (0.10 ± 0.03 mg/cm2/d), and no significant changes on the PET film surface were observed. The very low degradation rate of PET by PBATH Rf can be explained by the fact that the glass transition temperature (Tg ) of PET is about 70 °C, so that at milder temperatures (about 30 °C), the main PET chains have low motility and are less likely to undergo hydrolysis by PBATH Rf
[26]. Therefore, the compounds that were released to the supernatant from the PET film following the treatment by PBATH Rf likely derived from the degradation of the end of the polymer chain or loops that protrude from the films, which have higher mobility than the polymer chain backbone at mild conditions [58]. According to Kawai and co-workers [58], PBATH Rf could be classified as a PET surface-modifying enzyme.

In addition to catalyzing the hydrolysis of the aliphatic-aromatic polyester PBAT, PBATH Rf also showed hydrolytic activity toward other aliphatic polyesters, such as PESu, PBSA, PCL, and PBSu, which were hydrolyzed at even higher rates. This feature is common among other PBAT hydrolytic enzymes, such as Est1 [11], PCLE [17], CfCLE [18], PBATH Bp
[19], and Cut190* [13]. The degradation rate of PESu by PBATH Rf was the highest among all other polyesters tested, about 25-times faster than the rate of PBAT degradation. This is also supported by the experimental observation that the A-B ester bond was cleaved by PBATH Rf at approximately 19-fold higher rate than the T-B ester bond (Fig. 6). In addition, given that the binding energy between BAB and PBATH Rf is much lower than that between BTB and the enzyme, based on the docking model estimation, suggests that PBATH Rf holds higher-affinity to BAB than BTB. Taken together, these findings may help explain why PBATH Rf hydrolyzes aliphatic polyesters more efficiently compared with PBAT.

Qualitative analysis with LC-MS of water-soluble degradation products present in the buffer during the enzymatic degradation of PBAT film revealed that, besides other PBAT oligomers, the treatment with PBATH Rf released monomeric components such as 1,4-butanediol, adipic acid, and terephthalic acid, despite the fact that PBATH Rf cut the A-B bond more efficiently than the T-B bond (Fig. S10). This suggests that the enzyme could degrade PBAT to the monomeric constituents. A previous study has indicated that the strain NKCM2511 producing PBATH Rf grew on the medium containing 1,4-butanediol much faster than on that containing terephthalic acid and adipic acid [23]. Taken together, even if the strain NKCM2511 degrades PBAT by its enzyme PBATH Rf alone in moderate temperature environments, it is likely unable to mineralize the degraded products at a sufficiently high rate, so the final mineralization of the degraded products is probably achieved by the symbionts.

Of note, a previous study has shown that PBAT and its components are unable to induce PBATH Rf in R. fascians NKCM2511 [23]. It has also been suggested that the environmental degradation of PBAT does not affect the diversity of bacteria in the environment, although bacteria belonging to R. fascians are commonly known as pathogens of certain plants [42]. Thus, the fact that PBAT does not enrich specific bacteria in the soil suggests that PBAT can be used for the manufacture of agricultural gears such as mulching films, expected to be biodegraded after use [59]. In this study, although PBATH Rf was capable of hydrolyzing PBAT, the hydrolytic activity was relatively low. Therefore, in order to rapidly biodegrade PBAT, which is inherently slow to biodegrade in a moderate temperature environment, a mechanism to increase the number of various microbes, including PBAT-degraders around PBAT, might be necessary.
